source.title: NeuronFuzz: Safety Neuron Guided Fuzzing for LLM Safety Evaluation
source.authors: Zhiyuan Xu; Muhammad Firhard Roslan; Joseph Gardiner; Sana Belguith; Li-Chao Wu

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no garbling or truncation evident.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates whether adversarial jailbreak prompts can elicit harmful responses, using template fuzzing and attack-success evaluation rather than the original fine-tuning or per-token KL methods.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test harmful or benign fine-tuning, response-position KL concentration, compliant-prefix prefilling, decoding changes, or causal localization of safety in weights. Its directly relevant results are jailbreak discovery and transfer rates for adversarial prompts, including GCG suffix attacks. SafetyOracle classification and detection metrics concern internal signals or detection performance, not the behaviours named in the claim versions.
record.test_reason: Only the GCG baseline bears on a version. GCG appends an optimized suffix to a bare harmful payload, targeting an affirmative opening ('Sure, here is'). This is V4's suffix route. Table 3 reports how often GCG finds a jailbreak on five models. The main method (NeuronFuzz) and the other baselines rewrite whole prompt templates (role-play, refusal suppression). These are not prefills, suffixes or decoding changes, so those rows belong in fits_no_version. Nothing in the paper touches fine-tuning, per-token KL, causal weight localization, or deepening training.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that safety-neuron activations give dense, prefill-only feedback that improves jailbreak discovery and yields templates transferring across models, datasets and modalities. Perplexity and SmoothLLM defenses reduce but do not eliminate success. The SafetyOracle can also act as an input-side jailbreak detector.
record.recipe_differences: Uses internal activation scoring and adversarial prompt-template mutation; it does not fine-tune models or measure response-position KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Jailbreak discovery and transfer outcomes vary by model and target; transfer is weaker on some proprietary models. The paper also reports effects of input defenses, omitted from the extracted rows due to the row cap.

fits_no_version.finding: Template-wrapper and prompt-rewrite jailbreaks raise harmful compliance from near 0% to 76–100% JDR on five source models. Universal templates transfer to 14 targets at 17–86% top-1 ASR. Successful responses score 0.558 on the StrongREJECT rubric.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt-level role-play/template jailbreaks bypass refusal in safety-trained models and transfer across models.

fits_no_version.finding: A compact, stability-selected set of MLP neurons separates harmful from benign prompts (AUROC 0.969–0.999). Jailbreak templates lower its alarm score (Δwrap 0.031–0.195). The score correlates with jailbreak success (Spearman about -0.93 to -0.98).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful-intent recognition is readable from a small neuron subset, and jailbreak contexts suppress it (correlational, not causal localization).

record.problems: Attack evaluations use 100 harmful questions for the main source-model discovery results. Transfer results report five runs and uncertainty, but the paper's results concern adversarial jailbreak efficacy rather than the fine-tuning, KL, or causal-weight mechanisms in the claim.
record.rows_left_out: The 15 per-model defense-condition JDR results in Table 9 are omitted to stay within the 60-row limit; the extracted rows prioritize the main attack and transfer results. Other unrelated oracle classification/detection results are not rows for the tested claim version.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant start and decoding changes are not tested. Whether GCG successes actually produced the affirmative opening is not reported.
Safety neurons are chosen for a classifier probe; there is no causal test that they carry safety behaviour.

missing.what: GCG JDR under perplexity filter (6%) and SmoothLLM (10%) versus 91% with no defense, on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
Bare harmful-query baselines (Table 5 'Seeds' column; Table 15 baseline). These are the correct baselines for the GCG rows.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all template-based rows to V4. V4 concerns getting past the opening via prefill, suffix or decoding, so only the GCG baseline qualifies. The paper also argues, citing the original deep-alignment paper, that affirmative-prefix objectives are less reliable on recent aligned/reasoning models. That argument is not measured directly; the GCG numbers are consistent with it. GCG RGD and ETD are missing for GPT-OSS-20B because no success occurred.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples or measurement of refusal after such fine-tuning.
No benign-data fine-tuning or measurement of its effect on harmful compliance.
Tests adversarial jailbreak templates and a GCG suffix attack, but not compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes.
The paper selects neurons for an activation-based classifier, but does not causally test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Does not test whether data or training objectives cause safety shallowness.
Does not train or evaluate a method intended to deepen safety across response positions.
